chapter_title: Integrating with Enterprise IT and Hybrid Cloud
chapter_summary:
For many enterprises, a complete migration to the cloud is not a single event but a gradual journey, often resulting in a hybrid cloud architecture where on-premises infrastructure coexists with AWS. As a professional solutions architect, you will frequently be tasked with designing robust, secure, and performant integrations between these two environments. The foundation of any successful hybrid cloud strategy is connectivity. AWS offers several options, with **AWS Direct Connect** and **VPN (Virtual Private Network)** being the primary choices. Direct Connect provides a dedicated, private network connection from your on-premises data center to AWS, bypassing the public internet. This offers consistent network performance, reduced latency, and increased bandwidth, making it ideal for high-throughput, low-latency workloads, large data transfers, and applications requiring strict network predictability. Setting up Direct Connect involves working with an AWS Direct Connect partner, establishing a cross-connect, and configuring Virtual Interfaces (VIFs) to your VPCs or a Direct Connect Gateway.

While Direct Connect offers superior performance, it has a longer setup time and higher cost. For less demanding workloads, or as a backup for Direct Connect, **AWS Site-to-Site VPN** provides a secure, encrypted tunnel over the public internet. It's quicker to set up and more cost-effective for initial hybrid connectivity or for connecting smaller branch offices. You configure a Customer Gateway (your on-premises VPN device) and a Virtual Private Gateway (VPG) in AWS, then establish the IPSec VPN tunnel. A common mistake here is not configuring redundant VPN tunnels or using a single point of failure on the customer gateway side, which can lead to connectivity outages. Always design for high availability with multiple VPN tunnels to different VPG endpoints and redundant customer gateway devices.

As your hybrid environment grows, managing point-to-point connections between numerous VPCs and multiple on-premises networks can become complex and difficult to scale. This is where **AWS Transit Gateway** becomes indispensable. Transit Gateway acts as a central network hub, simplifying network architecture by allowing you to connect thousands of VPCs and on-premises networks to a single gateway. Instead of creating a mesh of individual connections, all traffic flows through the Transit Gateway. This centralizes routing, reduces operational overhead, and enables more granular network segmentation and security policies. For instance, you can connect your Direct Connect Gateway or VPN connections to the Transit Gateway, and then attach all your spoke VPCs to the same Transit Gateway, providing shared connectivity to your on-premises network. This also facilitates inter-VPC routing, allowing VPCs to communicate with each other through the Transit Gateway without peering connections.

Identity management is another critical aspect of hybrid integration. Many enterprises rely on on-premises Microsoft Active Directory for user authentication and authorization. **AWS Directory Service** offers several options to integrate with or extend your existing Active Directory. **AWS Managed Microsoft AD** provides a fully managed, highly available Active Directory on AWS, which can be seamlessly integrated with your on-premises AD using AD Connector or a trust relationship. **AD Connector** acts as a proxy, allowing your AWS services (like EC2, RDS, WorkSpaces) to authenticate users against your existing on-premises AD without syncing user data to AWS. This simplifies user management and maintains a single source of truth for identities. For new cloud-native applications or smaller organizations, **Simple AD** or a standalone AWS Managed Microsoft AD can be sufficient. The choice depends on your existing AD footprint, security requirements, and management overhead tolerance.

When migrating large datasets from on-premises to AWS, selecting the right data transfer mechanism is crucial for efficiency and cost-effectiveness. For petabyte-scale migrations, **AWS Snow Family** devices (Snowball Edge, Snowmobile) are often the most practical solution, physically shipping data to AWS. For online transfers, **AWS DataSync** provides a fast, secure, and automated way to move large amounts of data between on-premises storage (NFS, SMB, S3-compatible storage, Hadoop HDFS) and AWS storage services (S3, EFS, FSx for Windows File Server). DataSync handles scripting, scheduling, monitoring, and data integrity verification, significantly simplifying the migration process. For database migrations, **AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)** supports heterogeneous and homogeneous database migrations with minimal downtime. Understanding the volume of data, network bandwidth, acceptable downtime, and data sensitivity are key factors in choosing the appropriate transfer method.

Troubleshooting hybrid cloud environments requires a systematic approach. Connectivity issues often stem from misconfigured firewalls (on-premises or AWS Security Groups/NACLs), incorrect routing tables (VPC route tables, Transit Gateway route tables, on-premises router configurations), or BGP peering problems with Direct Connect/VPN. Tools like `traceroute`, `ping`, and `MTR` from both on-premises and AWS EC2 instances can help diagnose network path issues. Within AWS, **VPC Flow Logs** provide detailed information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces, invaluable for identifying blocked traffic. **AWS Network Access Analyzer** can help identify unintended network access paths. Always start by verifying the most basic connectivity and systematically check each layer of the network stack, from physical connections to routing and security policies.

screens.title: Integrating with Enterprise IT and Hybrid Cloud
screens.subtitle: Design secure, high-performance connections between on‑premises networks and AWS, and choose the right identity and data transfer strategies for hybrid environments.

narration.text: In this lesson we will make hybrid cloud feel practical and manageable. You will learn how to choose between private connections and encrypted tunnels, when a Transit Gateway makes a network manageable, how to extend your Active Directory to AWS, and which data transfer tools suit large migrations. We’ll use concrete examples like dedicated Direct Connect links for predictable performance, Site-to-Site VPN for rapid and cost-effective tunnels, and the Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke pattern to avoid a fragile mesh of peering links. You will also see how Snow devices, DataSync, and the Database Migration Service fit into different migration scenarios. Along the way I’ll call out common mistakes — like single points of failure in VPN setups — and practical checks such as using ping, traceroute, and VPC Flow Logs. By the end you should be able to recommend a hybrid connectivity approach, outline steps to attach VPCs and on-premises networks to a Transit Gateway, and pick an appropriate transfer mechanism for a given dataset size and downtime constraint. Think of this chapter as the playbook you’ll use when your organization must keep on-premises systems working with AWS without surprises.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Hybrid integration balances connectivity, identity, and data transfer choices so on‑premises systems and AWS work together reliably and securely.

Design secure connectivity, centralize routing, extend directory services, and choose efficient data transfer tools for hybrid migrations.

Connectivity patterns, identity integration, data migration choices.
Coming up

Goal
Confident hybrid design decisions with concrete steps.
Why this matters

Most enterprises run critical workloads that must remain accessible while teams adopt cloud services. Making the right choices up front reduces outages, simplifies operations, and lowers long‑term cost and effort.

Example

A financial app needs predictable latency and compliance controls. A dedicated Direct Connect circuit and Transit Gateway provide the predictable path and centralized routing required.

screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens you will gain practical skills to plan and operate hybrid cloud integrations. First, you will design secure and performant connectivity by choosing between AWS Direct Connect and Site‑to‑Site VPN, understanding tradeoffs in latency, throughput, setup time, and cost. Second, you will configure and manage AWS Transit Gateway so many VPCs and on‑prem networks can connect through a central hub instead of an unmanageable mesh. Third, you will map identity requirements to AWS Directory Service options, learning how AD Connector and AWS Managed Microsoft AD let on‑premises Active Directory persist as the source of truth. Fourth, you will evaluate data migration mechanisms and pick Snow Family, DataSync, or Database Migration Service according to volume, acceptable downtime, and network bandwidth. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember when to use each tool, and a verified competency milestone that describes what passing looks like in practice.

screens.title: Why connectivity is the foundation of hybrid cloud
screens.subtitle: Connectivity options and how they change security, performance, and operational tradeoffs

narration.text: Connectivity is the first decision you must make when planning a hybrid architecture, because it shapes performance, security, and operational cost. A dedicated private connection like AWS Direct Connect bypasses the public internet and brings predictable bandwidth and lower latency to critical applications. This predictability makes Direct Connect suitable for high‑throughput replication, low‑latency databases, or financial applications that need consistent response times. By contrast, a Site‑to‑Site VPN runs over the public internet using encrypted IPSec tunnels. It is faster to deploy and less expensive, making it ideal for branch sites, temporary proof‑of‑concept connections, or as a resilient backup to Direct Connect. A common misconception is thinking VPN is always sufficient; for workloads that require deterministic performance, the internet path will cause variable latency and jitter. Another mistake is assuming Direct Connect eliminates the need for good routing and security controls — you still must configure Virtual Interfaces, Direct Connect Gateway attachments, and route propagation correctly. Example: a development team might start with a VPN to connect offices quickly, then add Direct Connect for production databases and attach both to a Transit Gateway so traffic uses the private path when available and the VPN only as fallback. Takeaway: match the connectivity option to your workload’s performance, cost, and deployment-time needs, and plan redundancy from the start.

keyIdea.title: Connectivity claim
keyIdea.text: Direct Connect delivers predictable performance for demanding workloads; VPN is faster and cheaper to set up and useful as primary or backup depending on requirements.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Why connectivity is the foundation
Definition

Connectivity is the network fabric linking on‑premises systems and AWS. It determines latency, bandwidth, and the predictability of traffic between locations.

Comparison
Direct Connect
Dedicated, private connection. Predictable performance and improved throughput.
Site-to-Site VPN
IPSec tunnel over the internet. Fast setup and cost-effective for many use cases.
Common mistake
Relying on a single VPN tunnel or a single customer gateway device creates a single point of failure for connectivity.
Key takeaway
Match connection type to workload: prioritize Direct Connect for predictable, high‑throughput needs and use VPN for rapid or backup connectivity.
Scenario cards
Production database replication
Needs consistent latency and high bandwidth for replication and queries. Direct Connect is preferable because it avoids internet variability.
Branch office access
Branch offices or development teams need quick access with limited budget. A Site-to-Site VPN provides encrypted connectivity quickly and cost-effectively.
Mixed deployment
Combine Direct Connect for critical traffic and a VPN as fallback. Use routing and Transit Gateway to prefer the private path while keeping a resilient tunnel available.

screens.title: Setting up AWS Direct Connect and Virtual Interfaces
screens.subtitle: Steps, partners, and VIF configuration for private connectivity

narration.text: Setting up Direct Connect requires planning and coordination with a partner or provider because it establishes a physical cross‑connect into AWS. The process begins by ordering a Direct Connect location and arranging a cross‑connect with a partner. Once the circuit is available, you create a Direct Connect connection in AWS and then configure Virtual Interfaces, or VIFs. A private VIF connects to a VPC via a Direct Connect Gateway, providing private access to your VPC CIDRs. You may also create public VIFs to access public AWS services over the dedicated link. It’s important to plan Virtual Interface capacity and tag VIFs so they map cleanly to application or account boundaries. A common misconception is that Direct Connect removes the need for routing rules — you must still manage BGP sessions, propagate routes, and ensure your on‑premises router advertises correct prefixes. Example: after ordering a physical circuit, create a private VIF to a Direct Connect Gateway, then attach that gateway to your Transit Gateway so multiple VPCs can share the connection. Always validate via BGP status and test throughput to confirm the link meets expectations. The core outcome is a predictable, high-throughput path that your applications can rely on.

keyIdea.title: Direct Connect setup
keyIdea.text: Order a physical circuit, create a Direct Connect connection, configure private VIFs and BGP routing, and attach via a Direct Connect Gateway to VPCs or Transit Gateway.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Setting up AWS Direct Connect
Step-by-step
Order circuit and coordinate with partner
Arrange cross-connect at a Direct Connect location.
Create Direct Connect connection and VIF
Define private VIF for VPC access and public VIF for AWS public endpoints if needed.
Configure BGP and Direct Connect Gateway
Advertise prefixes and attach the Direct Connect Gateway to VPCs or Transit Gateway.
Validate and test performance
Check BGP session status, measure throughput, and confirm route propagation.
Example mapping
After provisioning a Direct Connect circuit, create a private VIF to a Direct Connect Gateway. Attach that gateway to your Transit Gateway so multiple VPCs can share the dedicated path without individual VIFs per VPC. Monitor BGP for stability.
Key Takeaway
Direct Connect requires physical provisioning and BGP setup; it delivers predictable bandwidth but still needs routing discipline.

screens.title: Site-to-Site VPN: quick, encrypted connectivity
screens.subtitle: How VPN tunnels work and patterns for high availability

narration.text: Site-to-Site VPN provides an encrypted IPSec tunnel between your on‑premises customer gateway device and AWS. It is typically faster to stand up than Direct Connect, so teams use it for proof‑of‑concept work, branch connectivity, and as a resilient backup to a private link. Setting up a VPN involves creating a Customer Gateway representing your on‑prem router and a Virtual Private Gateway or Transit Gateway as the AWS endpoint, then establishing IPSec tunnels with either static routes or dynamic routing using BGP. Critical operational guidance is to deploy redundant tunnels and redundant customer gateway devices so a single device failure or tunnel flap does not take down your connectivity. A common misconception is assuming one tunnel is enough. In practice, create at least two tunnels to distinct endpoints or at least two customer gateway devices. Example: configure two tunnels to your Transit Gateway and verify both are up; if one fails, BGP will prefer the remaining path. Also allow the required IPSec UDP ports through security devices and check route tables in both environments. Takeaway: VPNs are flexible and fast but require HA planning to be production-ready.

keyIdea.title: VPN pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Site-to-Site VPN for quick encrypted connectivity, but always design for redundant tunnels and devices for production reliability.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Site-to-Site VPN
How it works
  • Define a Customer Gateway representing your on‑premises VPN device and its public IP.
  • Create a VPN connection to a Virtual Private Gateway or to a Transit Gateway as the AWS endpoint.
  • Establish IPSec tunnels and configure static routes or BGP for dynamic routing.
Best practice
Deploy at least two tunnels and, where possible, redundant customer gateway devices to avoid single points of failure.
Example checklist
Create Customer Gateway
Record the public IP of your on‑prem VPN device and choose BGP or static routing.
Create VPN connection
Select the Transit Gateway as the AWS target to centralize routing for multiple VPCs.
Configure on-prem device
Download VPN configuration from the console and apply IPSec settings. Allow UDP 500 and 4500 where necessary.
Key Takeaway
VPNs are fast to deploy and flexible; make them production-ready by adding redundancy and checking route tables.

screens.title: AWS Transit Gateway: centralizing connectivity
screens.subtitle: Hub-and-spoke routing for scalable multi-VPC and on-prem connectivity

narration.text: AWS Transit Gateway provides a central hub that simplifies connectivity as your cloud footprint grows. Instead of building a mesh of peering links or multiple discrete VPNs, attach VPCs and on‑premises connections to a Transit Gateway and manage routing centrally. This reduces operational complexity and makes it easier to enforce segmentation and security across many accounts or environments. Transit Gateway also lets you attach Direct Connect Gateway and VPN connections, which makes a single dedicated circuit usable by many VPCs. A common contrast is the mesh approach: with N VPCs, peering requires N*(N-1)/2 connections, whereas a Transit Gateway needs only N attachments. Example: attach ProdVPC and DevVPC to a Transit Gateway, attach your Site‑to‑Site VPN or Direct Connect Gateway to the same Transit Gateway, and then use route table association and propagation to control which VPCs can reach on‑premises networks. Misconceptions include thinking Transit Gateway magically fixes all routing errors — you must still set route tables and consider route propagation and isolation via separate Transit Gateway route tables. Takeaway: use Transit Gateway to centralize routing, simplify expansion, and enable shared, controlled access between AWS and on‑premises networks.

keyIdea.title: Transit Gateway value
keyIdea.text: Transit Gateway simplifies scaling by providing a central hub for VPCs and on‑prem attachments, avoiding the complexity of a full mesh.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › AWS Transit Gateway
Hub-and-spoke pattern
Attach many VPCs and on-premises connections to a single Transit Gateway. Manage routing via Transit Gateway route tables and control segmentation by creating multiple route tables when needed.
Scale benefit
Avoid N-squared peering complexity; add new attachments without reconfiguring each VPC pair.
Inter-VPC routing
VPCs attached to the same Transit Gateway can communicate through it without peering connections.
Integration
Connect Direct Connect Gateway or Site-to-Site VPN attachments to provide on-premises access to all spokes.
Segmentation
Use multiple Transit Gateway route tables to isolate environments like Prod, Dev, and Shared Services.
Concrete example
Create a Transit Gateway, attach ProdVPC (10.1.0.0/16) and DevVPC (10.2.0.0/16), then attach your Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect Gateway. Update VPC route tables to point on‑premises CIDR ranges to the Transit Gateway attachment. Optionally propagate routes so the Transit Gateway learns on‑premises prefixes via BGP.
Key Takeaway
Transit Gateway centralizes routing for scale. It reduces peering complexity and enables shared access patterns when configured with appropriate route tables and propagation rules.

screens.title: Integrating on‑premises Active Directory with AWS
screens.subtitle: AD Connector, AWS Managed Microsoft AD, and design considerations

narration.text: Identity drives authentication and authorization across hybrid systems, and many enterprises maintain Microsoft Active Directory on‑premises as the authoritative identity store. AWS Directory Service provides options to integrate with that directory without forcing a full migration. AD Connector acts as a proxy: it does not sync directory data to AWS but forwards authentication requests to your on‑premises AD, which keeps a single source of truth and reduces directory replication. AWS Managed Microsoft AD provides a fully managed Active Directory hosted by AWS; you can establish a trust relationship or replicate accounts depending on your security needs. Simple AD or a standalone managed AD may fit smaller organizations or cloud‑native applications that do not require on‑premises integration. A common misconception is thinking AD Connector replicates accounts — it does not; instead it proxies authentication. Example: use AD Connector for EC2 login and RDS Windows authentication when you want on‑premises credentials to remain authoritative without syncing. Consider network latency, connectivity, and trust relationships when designing the integration because authentication latency can affect application login performance. Takeaway: pick AD Connector when you need a low-management proxy to on‑premises AD, and choose Managed Microsoft AD when you need a cloud-hosted directory with AWS-managed availability.

keyIdea.title: Identity options
keyIdea.text: AD Connector proxies authentication to your on‑premises AD; Managed Microsoft AD provides a managed AD in AWS for trust or standalone scenarios.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Integrating Active Directory
Service options
AD Connector
A proxy that forwards authentication to on‑premises AD without syncing user accounts to AWS.
AWS Managed Microsoft AD
A fully managed, highly available AD hosted on AWS that can be trusted or used standalone.
Simple AD / standalone
Suitable for small or cloud-native setups where on‑premises integration is not required.
Design considerations
  • Decide whether you need proxy authentication or a managed directory in AWS.
  • Factor in latency and connectivity: authentication calls traverse the network and affect login times.
  • Consider management overhead: AD Connector reduces replication but increases dependency on on‑premises uptime.
Key Takeaway
Use AD Connector to keep a single on‑premises source of truth without syncing accounts; use Managed Microsoft AD when you need AWS-hosted directory services.

screens.title: Choosing data transfer mechanisms
screens.subtitle: Snow Family, DataSync, and Database Migration Service — when to use each

narration.text: Transferring large amounts of data into AWS requires choosing the right mechanism to balance time, cost, and complexity. For petabyte-scale datasets, physical appliances in the Snow Family — like Snowball Edge or Snowmobile — are often the practical solution because they avoid long online transfer times and network saturation. For automated online file transfers, DataSync moves data from NFS, SMB, or compatible object stores to S3, EFS, or FSx and handles scheduling, integrity checks, and performance tuning. For databases, AWS Database Migration Service supports homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations with minimal downtime using continuous replication and change data capture. The decision factors are dataset volume, available network bandwidth, acceptable downtime, and data sensitivity. A common misconception is assuming online transfer is always faster; in many cases a Snow device physically shipped to AWS completes a petabyte transfer faster and with lower network cost. Example: if you must move several petabytes and your WAN is limited, order a Snow device. If you need continuous sync of a file system with validation, set up DataSync jobs. If moving a production database with minimal downtime, configure DMS with replication and a cutover plan. Takeaway: match tool to scale and operational constraints rather than defaulting to online transfer.

keyIdea.title: Transfer principle
keyIdea.text: Use Snow Family for very large physical transfers, DataSync for automated file-level transfers, and DMS for database migrations with minimal downtime.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Choosing data transfer mechanisms
Tool summary
Snow Family
Physical devices for terabytes or petabytes; ship data to AWS when network transfer is impractical.
DataSync
Automated online transfer for file systems and object stores with scheduling and data integrity checks.
Database Migration Service
Migrate databases with minimal downtime using continuous replication and change data capture.
Decision factors
  • Volume of data: small, large, or petabyte-scale favors different approaches.
  • Network bandwidth: constrained links often point to Snow devices.
  • Acceptable downtime: DMS supports near-zero downtime migrations for databases.
  • Data integrity and automation: DataSync provides scheduling and verification for files.
Scenario: Petabyte archive
Order a Snow device to avoid saturating your WAN and speed the transfer.
Scenario: File server sync
Use DataSync to move files to S3 or EFS, with validation and scheduling.
Key Takeaway
Select transfer tooling by volume, bandwidth, and downtime requirements rather than defaulting to online copy for large datasets.

screens.title: Troubleshooting hybrid network issues
screens.subtitle: Systematic checks from physical links to routing and security policies

narration.text: Troubleshooting hybrid connectivity requires a layered, systematic approach. Start at the physical layer: verify circuit status for Direct Connect or tunnel state for VPNs. Then check routing configuration — VPC route tables, Transit Gateway route tables, and on‑premises router advertisements via BGP — to ensure each side knows how to reach the other. Security is another frequent cause: confirm Security Groups, Network ACLs, and on‑premises firewall rules are not blocking traffic, and that IPSec UDP ports are allowed when using VPN. Use tools like ping and traceroute or MTR from both an on‑premises host and an EC2 instance in a private subnet to observe where packets stop. Within AWS, enable VPC Flow Logs to see whether traffic is reaching network interfaces and whether it is being denied. AWS Network Access Analyzer can reveal unintended paths or reachability that you did not plan for. A common misconception is to jump straight to application logs — while useful, start by confirming basic network reachability first. Example troubleshooting workflow: verify tunnel state in the console, run traceroute from both ends, examine VPC Flow Logs to find denied traffic, and check Transit Gateway route table propagation. Takeaway: debug from physical to routing to security, using network tools and AWS diagnostics at each layer.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting approach
keyIdea.text: Work from physical connections to routing to security, and use traceroute, VPC Flow Logs, and Network Access Analyzer to isolate the issue.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Troubleshooting hybrid networks
Systematic checklist
  1. Verify physical status: Direct Connect circuit state or VPN tunnel status.
  2. Validate routing: BGP sessions, route tables, and route propagation in Transit Gateway.
  3. Check security: security groups, NACLs, and on‑premises firewall rules.
  4. Use network tools: ping, traceroute, and MTR from both sides to see where packets stop.
  5. Review AWS diagnostics: VPC Flow Logs and Network Access Analyzer for blocked traffic or unexpected paths.
Example quick commands
# From an on-prem host
ping 10.1.0.10
traceroute 10.1.0.10

# From an EC2 in a private subnet
ping 192.168.10.5
traceroute 192.168.10.5
Key Takeaway
Start with basic reachability checks, then validate routing and security policies, and use AWS logging to locate blocked traffic.

screens.title: Hands-on: Simulating Site-to-Site VPN with Transit Gateway
screens.subtitle: Terminal-first steps to create VPCs, Transit Gateway, VPN, and test connectivity

narration.text: This walkthrough guides you through a simulated lab where you create two VPCs, a Transit Gateway, and a Site‑to‑Site VPN attachment, then validate connectivity using simple network tools. The scenario uses ProdVPC with CIDR 10.1.0.0/16 and DevVPC with 10.2.0.0/16 plus a simulated on‑prem VPC of 192.168.0.0/16. The main steps are: create VPCs and private EC2 instances to act as application servers, create a Transit Gateway and attach the VPCs, create a Customer Gateway using the public IP of your simulated on‑prem device, and then create a VPN connection to the Transit Gateway. After tunnels report as up, update the private subnet route tables to route the on‑premises CIDR to the Transit Gateway attachment and verify by running ping and traceroute between the simulated on‑prem host and the EC2 instances. A common pitfall is forgetting to enable association and propagation on attachments or neglecting to add the on‑prem CIDR to the VPC route table. Example terminal commands are provided in the visual panel; use them to simulate pings and traceroutes and confirm reachability. End by cleaning up resources to avoid charges. This exercise makes the abstractions concrete and gives you a repeatable validation routine.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Create VPCs, attach them to a Transit Gateway, add a VPN connection via a Customer Gateway, and validate end‑to‑end connectivity with ping and traceroute.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Lab: Site-to-Site VPN with Transit Gateway
Starter terminal commands (simulated)
# Create VPCs (example CIDRs)
# ProdVPC: 10.1.0.0/16
# DevVPC: 10.2.0.0/16
# OnPremVPC: 192.168.0.0/16 (simulated)

# Create Transit Gateway
# aws ec2 create-transit-gateway --description "TGW for hybrid lab"

# Create TGW attachments for Prod and Dev
# aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxxx --vpc-id vpc-prod --subnet-ids subnet-priv-prod

# Create Customer Gateway using public IP of simulated device
# aws ec2 create-customer-gateway --type ipsec.1 --public-ip 198.51.100.10 --bgp-asn 65000

# Create VPN connection to Transit Gateway
# aws ec2 create-vpn-connection --customer-gateway-id cgw-xxxx --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxxx --type ipsec.1 --options '{"StaticRoutesOnly":false}'

# After tunnels are Up, update private route tables to point on-prem CIDR to TGW attachment

# Test connectivity from simulated on-prem host
# ping 10.1.0.10

screens.title: Direct Connect vs. VPN — decision matrix
screens.subtitle: Compare performance, setup time, cost, and use cases to decide which to recommend

narration.text: When advising stakeholders, frame the Direct Connect versus VPN decision in terms of performance needs, delivery time, and cost. Direct Connect: predictable bandwidth, lower latency, best for critical, high‑throughput applications, but it takes longer to provision and typically costs more. Site‑to‑Site VPN: quick to deploy and lower initial cost, ideal for pilots, branch offices, and as a backup link. Think about hybrid patterns: you can use both — Direct Connect for primary traffic and VPN as a secondary resilient path. Stakeholders often assume that higher cost always means better security; while Direct Connect avoids the public internet, you still need strong routing, access control, and encryption where required. Use the following decision criteria: if you require determinism for latency and throughput and can tolerate longer lead time and higher cost, recommend Direct Connect. If you need speed of deployment or budget constraints, recommend VPN and plan for a future Direct Connect if demand grows. Example: a trading system will almost always need Direct Connect for predictability, whereas a distributed dev team can start with VPN. Always include redundancy planning and route failover scenarios in your recommendation.

keyIdea.title: Decision matrix
keyIdea.text: Direct Connect for deterministic performance and high throughput; VPN for fast, cost-effective deployments and as a resilient backup.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Direct Connect vs. VPN
Side-by-side
Direct Connect
Predictable, private, high-throughput. Longer provisioning lead time and higher cost.
Site-to-Site VPN
Encrypted over internet, fast to deploy, cost-effective. Performance can vary with internet conditions.
Decision guide
  • Need deterministic latency and high bandwidth → Direct Connect.
  • Need rapid deployment or lower cost → Site-to-Site VPN.
  • Hybrid approach → Direct Connect primary, VPN fallback.
Key Takeaway
Frame the recommendation around performance needs, time to provision, and cost, and include redundancy in either choice.

screens.title: Activity walkthrough: Establish VPN + Transit Gateway (cleanup plan)
screens.subtitle: Complete the lab scenario and safely clean up resources to avoid charges

narration.text: This final lesson brings the lab full circle by outlining the cleanup and verification steps after you simulate hybrid connectivity. After creating your VPCs, Transit Gateway, attachments, and VPN connection, validate connectivity with ping and traceroute to ensure traffic flows in both directions. Confirm BGP sessions where used and check that Transit Gateway route tables have the expected propagated routes. For cleanup, delete the VPN connection and Customer Gateway, detach and delete Transit Gateway attachments, delete the Transit Gateway if it is no longer required, terminate EC2 instances, and finally delete the VPCs created for the lab. A common mistake is forgetting to remove Transit Gateway attachments before deleting the Transit Gateway; AWS will prevent deletion until attachments are removed. Also remember to remove any related Elastic IPs or gateways that incur charges. Example cleanup checklist: verify no active tunnels, remove VPN attachments from the Transit Gateway, delete the Transit Gateway only after all attachments are gone, then delete VPCs. The takeaway is that one responsible lab session includes both verification and a clean teardown to keep your environment tidy and costs under control.

keyIdea.title: Lab cleanup
keyIdea.text: Validate connectivity, then remove VPNs, detach TGW attachments, and delete TGW and VPCs in the correct order to avoid orphaned charges.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Activity walkthrough & cleanup
Verification checklist
  1. Confirm VPN tunnels are UP in the console.
  2. Run ping and traceroute between simulated on-prem and VPC EC2s.
  3. Validate Transit Gateway route table propagation and associations.
  4. Check Security Groups and NACLs for allowed traffic during tests.
Cleanup steps
1. Delete VPN connection and Customer Gateway.
2. Detach and delete Transit Gateway attachments.
3. Delete Transit Gateway after attachments are removed.
4. Terminate EC2 instances and delete VPCs and subnets.
Common mistake
Attempting to delete a Transit Gateway while attachments exist will fail; remove attachments first to prevent orphaned resources and charges.

narration.text: Let’s summarize the essentials you should remember. First, connectivity choices are foundational: choose Direct Connect for predictable, high‑throughput paths and Site‑to‑Site VPN for speed of deployment and cost efficiency. Second, Transit Gateway centralizes routing across multiple VPCs and on‑premises networks, simplifying scale and reducing peering complexity. Third, identity integration matters: AD Connector proxies authentication to on‑premises Active Directory while AWS Managed Microsoft AD provides a managed directory option in AWS. These are the primary building blocks you will combine when designing hybrid cloud solutions. Keep the decision criteria—performance, provisioning time, cost, and redundancy—front and center when you recommend a connectivity approach. Use the appropriate data transfer tool for the dataset size and required downtime, and always include verification and cleanup steps in lab exercises. With these concepts, you can produce robust hybrid designs that balance operational needs with security and cost constraints.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Connectivity, centralized routing, identity integration, and the right transfer tool together form a practical hybrid integration strategy.

Hybrid Cloud
Combines on‑premises infrastructure with AWS so systems can interoperate.
Direct Connect
A dedicated private connection that bypasses the internet for predictable performance.
Site-to-Site VPN
Encrypted tunnel over the internet, quick to deploy and good for backups or branch connectivity.
Summary takeaway

Match connectivity and transfer choices to workload needs, centralize routing with Transit Gateway as you scale, and integrate identity in a way that preserves a single source of truth.

screens.subtitle: Compact glossary of key services and their role

narration.text: A short glossary helps you keep service roles straight. Transit Gateway is your central hub for routing across many VPCs and on‑prem networks. AWS Directory Service gives you options to either proxy authentication to on‑premises AD using AD Connector or run a managed Active Directory in AWS with AWS Managed Microsoft AD. For data movement, Snow Family handles very large physical transfers, DataSync automates file synchronization, and Database Migration Service migrates databases with minimal downtime. When designing hybrid systems, always state the expected traffic pattern, performance needs, and acceptable downtime, and then pick the service combination that meets those constraints. Keep redundancy, route propagation, and security controls in your architecture notes so your designs remain operationally robust.
